title: Interview Score Distribution
markdown:
### The Scenario
An HR analyst wants to understand how candidate interview scores are distributed before setting a screening threshold.

### The Task
- Use `plt.hist()` to create a histogram of `scores`.
- Use exactly `6` bins.
- Set the bar color to `orange`.
- Set the edge color to `black`.
- Set the x-axis label to `Score`.
- Set the title to `Interview Score Distribution`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

scores = [58, 61, 64, 67, 68, 70, 72, 73, 75, 78, 81, 84, 86, 89, 91, 94]

# Create your chart below



plt.show()
validation_code:
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.patches) == 6, 'We expected a histogram with exactly 6 bins.'
patch = ax.patches[0]
assert mcolors.to_rgba(patch.get_facecolor()) == mcolors.to_rgba('orange'), 'Set the histogram bar color to orange.'
assert mcolors.to_rgba(patch.get_edgecolor()) == mcolors.to_rgba('black'), 'Set the histogram edge color to black.'
assert ax.get_xlabel() == 'Score', 'Set the x-axis label to exactly "Score".'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Interview Score Distribution', 'Set the title to exactly "Interview Score Distribution".'
hints: This is still a histogram task, but now the bar styling matters too.
Use `plt.hist()` with `bins`, `color`, and `edgecolor`, then add `plt.xlabel()`.
Try `plt.hist(scores, bins=6, color='orange', edgecolor='black')`, then `plt.xlabel('Score')` and `plt.title('Interview Score Distribution')`.
solution_code:
plt.hist(scores, bins=6, color='orange', edgecolor='black')
plt.xlabel('Score')
plt.title('Interview Score Distribution')

title: Workout Duration Comparison
markdown:
### The Scenario
A fitness studio wants to compare the distribution of workout durations for morning and evening members.

### The Task
- Plot `morning_minutes` and `evening_minutes` on the same histogram.
- Use `5` bins for each histogram.
- Add labels `Morning` and `Evening` so the legend is correct.
- Show the legend.
- Set the title to `Workout Duration Comparison`.
- Display the chart.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

morning_minutes = [20, 22, 25, 28, 30, 32, 35, 38]
evening_minutes = [25, 27, 29, 31, 34, 36, 39, 42]

# Create your chart below



plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.patches) == 10, 'We expected two histograms with 5 bins each.'
legend = ax.get_legend()
assert legend is not None, 'Show the legend using plt.legend().' 
labels = {text.get_text() for text in legend.get_texts()}
assert labels == {'Morning', 'Evening'}, 'The legend labels must be Morning and Evening.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Workout Duration Comparison', 'Set the title to exactly "Workout Duration Comparison".'
hints: You need both groups drawn on the same axes so their distributions can be compared directly.
Use `plt.hist()` twice with `label=` for each group, then call `plt.legend()`.
Try `plt.hist(morning_minutes, bins=5, label='Morning')` and `plt.hist(evening_minutes, bins=5, label='Evening')`, then `plt.legend()` and `plt.title('Workout Duration Comparison')`.
solution_code:
plt.hist(morning_minutes, bins=5, label='Morning')
plt.hist(evening_minutes, bins=5, label='Evening')
plt.legend()
plt.title('Workout Duration Comparison')

title: Revenue and Orders Subplot
markdown:
### The Scenario
A small business wants one figure that shows monthly revenue beside the distribution of customer order counts.

### The Task
- Create a `1x2` subplot layout.
- In the first subplot, plot `months` vs `revenue` as a line chart.
- Set the first subplot title to `Revenue`.
- In the second subplot, create a histogram of `orders` using `4` bins.
- Set the second subplot title to `Orders`.
- Display the full figure.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr']
revenue = [200, 230, 250, 280]
orders = [18, 20, 22, 24, 25, 27, 28, 30]

# Create your figure below



plt.show()
validation_code:
fig = plt.gcf()
assert len(fig.axes) == 2, 'Create exactly two subplots.'
left_ax, right_ax = fig.axes
assert len(left_ax.lines) == 1, 'The first subplot should contain a line chart.'
assert len(right_ax.patches) == 4, 'The second subplot should contain a histogram with 4 bins.'
assert left_ax.get_title() == 'Revenue', 'Set the first subplot title to exactly "Revenue".'
assert right_ax.get_title() == 'Orders', 'Set the second subplot title to exactly "Orders".'
hints: This figure needs two panels placed side by side.
Use `plt.subplot()` or `plt.subplots()` to create a `1x2` layout, then draw one chart in each axis.
Try `plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)` with `plt.plot(months, revenue)` and `plt.title('Revenue')`, then `plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)` with `plt.hist(orders, bins=4)` and `plt.title('Orders')`.
solution_code:
plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.plot(months, revenue)
plt.title('Revenue')
plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
plt.hist(orders, bins=4)
plt.title('Orders')

title: Traffic and Purchase Value Dashboard
markdown:
### The Scenario
An ecommerce analyst wants a simple vertical dashboard showing daily site visits and the distribution of purchase values.

### The Task
- Set the figure size to `(8, 6)`.
- Create a `2x1` subplot layout.
- In the top subplot, plot `days` vs `visits`.
- Set the top subplot title to `Website Visits`.
- In the bottom subplot, create a histogram of `purchase_values` using `5` bins.
- Set the bottom subplot title to `Purchase Values`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

days = ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri']
visits = [120, 145, 138, 160, 172]
purchase_values = [18, 22, 25, 30, 35, 40, 42, 45, 48, 50, 55]

# Create your figure below



plt.show()
validation_code:
fig = plt.gcf()
width, height = fig.get_size_inches()
assert abs(width - 8) < 0.1 and abs(height - 6) < 0.1, 'Set the figure size to 8 by 6.'
assert len(fig.axes) == 2, 'Create exactly two subplots.'
top_ax, bottom_ax = fig.axes
assert len(top_ax.lines) == 1, 'The top subplot should contain a line chart.'
assert len(bottom_ax.patches) == 5, 'The bottom subplot should contain a histogram with 5 bins.'
assert top_ax.get_title() == 'Website Visits', 'Set the top subplot title to exactly "Website Visits".'
assert bottom_ax.get_title() == 'Purchase Values', 'Set the bottom subplot title to exactly "Purchase Values".'
hints: You need a taller figure with one subplot stacked above the other.
Use `plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))` and a `2x1` subplot layout.

Try `plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))`, then `plt.subplot(2, 1, 1)` with `plt.plot(days, visits)` and `plt.title('Website Visits')`, then `plt.subplot(2, 1, 2)` with `plt.hist(purchase_values, bins=5)` and `plt.title('Purchase Values')`.
solution_code:
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.subplot(2, 1, 1)
plt.plot(days, visits)
plt.title('Website Visits')
plt.subplot(2, 1, 2)
plt.hist(purchase_values, bins=5)
plt.title('Purchase Values')

title: Mini Business Dashboard
markdown:
### The Scenario
A startup founder wants a compact visual dashboard with four quick views of business performance.

### The Task
- Create a `2x2` subplot layout.
- In subplot 1, create a line chart of `days` vs `sales` titled `Sales Line`.
- In subplot 2, create a scatter plot of `ad_spend` vs `signups` titled `Ad Spend vs Signups`.
- In subplot 3, create a bar chart of `regions` vs `region_sales` titled `Regional Sales`.
- In subplot 4, create a histogram of `ratings` with `4` bins titled `Ratings Histogram`.
- Display the full figure.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

days = ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu']
sales = [20, 24, 19, 27]
ad_spend = [100, 120, 90, 140]
signups = [5, 7, 4, 8]
regions = ['North', 'South', 'East', 'West']
region_sales = [80, 65, 70, 90]
ratings = [3, 4, 5, 4, 3, 5, 4, 4]

# Create your dashboard below



plt.show()
validation_code:
fig = plt.gcf()
assert len(fig.axes) == 4, 'Create exactly four subplots in a 2x2 layout.'
ax1, ax2, ax3, ax4 = fig.axes
assert len(ax1.lines) == 1, 'The first subplot should contain a line chart.'
assert len(ax2.collections) > 0, 'The second subplot should contain a scatter plot.'
assert len(ax3.patches) == 4, 'The third subplot should contain a bar chart with four bars.'
assert len(ax4.patches) == 4, 'The fourth subplot should contain a histogram with 4 bins.'
assert ax1.get_title() == 'Sales Line', 'Set the first subplot title to exactly "Sales Line".'
assert ax2.get_title() == 'Ad Spend vs Signups', 'Set the second subplot title to exactly "Ad Spend vs Signups".'
assert ax3.get_title() == 'Regional Sales', 'Set the third subplot title to exactly "Regional Sales".'
assert ax4.get_title() == 'Ratings Histogram', 'Set the fourth subplot title to exactly "Ratings Histogram".'
hints: Treat this as four small charts inside one figure.
Use a `2x2` subplot layout and place one chart type in each panel.

Try `plt.subplot(2, 2, 1)` with `plt.plot(...)`, `plt.subplot(2, 2, 2)` with `plt.scatter(...)`, `plt.subplot(2, 2, 3)` with `plt.bar(...)`, and `plt.subplot(2, 2, 4)` with `plt.hist(ratings, bins=4)`.
solution_code:
plt.subplot(2, 2, 1)
plt.plot(days, sales)
plt.title('Sales Line')
plt.subplot(2, 2, 2)
plt.scatter(ad_spend, signups)
plt.title('Ad Spend vs Signups')
plt.subplot(2, 2, 3)
plt.bar(regions, region_sales)
plt.title('Regional Sales')
plt.subplot(2, 2, 4)
plt.hist(ratings, bins=4)
plt.title('Ratings Histogram')

title: Delivery Time Histogram with Mean Line
markdown:
### The Scenario
A logistics team wants to visualize delivery times and clearly mark the average delivery time.

### The Task
- Create a histogram of `delivery_times` using `6` bins.
- Add a vertical dashed line at the mean delivery time.
- Set the title to `Delivery Times`.
- Set the x-axis label to `Minutes`.
- Display the chart.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

delivery_times = [22, 24, 25, 27, 29, 30, 31, 33, 35, 36, 38, 40]

# Create your chart below



plt.show()
validation_code:
import numpy as np
ax = plt.gca()
expected_mean = np.mean(delivery_times)
assert len(ax.patches) == 6, 'We expected a histogram with exactly 6 bins.'
assert any(np.allclose(line.get_xdata(), [expected_mean, expected_mean]) for line in ax.lines), 'Add a vertical line at the mean using plt.axvline().' 
assert ax.get_title() == 'Delivery Times', 'Set the title to exactly "Delivery Times".'
assert ax.get_xlabel() == 'Minutes', 'Set the x-axis label to exactly "Minutes".'
hints: First build the histogram, then compute and mark the average as a guide line.
Use `plt.hist()` for the bins and `plt.axvline()` for the mean line.
Try `plt.hist(delivery_times, bins=6)`, then `plt.axvline(np.mean(delivery_times), linestyle='--')`, `plt.title('Delivery Times')`, and `plt.xlabel('Minutes')`.
solution_code:
plt.hist(delivery_times, bins=6)
plt.axvline(np.mean(delivery_times), linestyle='--')
plt.title('Delivery Times')
plt.xlabel('Minutes')

title: Study Hours Relationship Scatter
markdown:
### The Scenario
An instructor wants a scatter plot that highlights the relationship between study time and exam performance.

### The Task
- Use `plt.scatter()` to plot `study_hours` vs `exam_score`.
- Set the marker color to `red`.
- Set the title to `Study Time and Exam Score`.
- Set the x-axis label to `Study Hours`.
- Set the y-axis label to `Exam Score`.
- Display the chart.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

study_hours = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
exam_score = [52, 58, 63, 70, 76, 84, 90]

# Create your chart below



plt.show()
validation_code:
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.collections) > 0, 'We could not find a scatter plot. Did you use plt.scatter()?'
facecolors = ax.collections[0].get_facecolors()
assert len(facecolors) > 0 and mcolors.to_rgba(facecolors[0]) == mcolors.to_rgba('red'), 'Set the scatter marker color to red.'

assert ax.get_xlabel() == 'Study Hours', 'Set the x-axis label to exactly "Study Hours".'
assert ax.get_ylabel() == 'Exam Score', 'Set the y-axis label to exactly "Exam Score".'
hints: A scatter plot is best when you want to show the relationship between two numeric variables.
Use `plt.scatter()` and set the point color with `color='red'`.
Try `plt.scatter(study_hours, exam_score, color='red')`, then add `plt.title('Study Time and Exam Score')`, `plt.xlabel('Study Hours')`, and `plt.ylabel('Exam Score')`.
solution_code:
plt.scatter(study_hours, exam_score, color='red')
plt.title('Study Time and Exam Score')
plt.xlabel('Study Hours')
plt.ylabel('Exam Score')

title: Customer Satisfaction Boxplot
markdown:
### The Scenario
A service team wants to compare customer satisfaction scores across support channels using a simple summary chart.

### The Task
- Use `plt.boxplot()` to create a boxplot with the three score lists in the order `chat_scores`, `email_scores`, `phone_scores`.
- Set the x-axis tick labels to `Chat`, `Email`, and `Phone`.
- Set the title to `Customer Satisfaction by Channel`.
- Set the y-axis label to `Satisfaction Score`.
- Display the chart.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

chat_scores = [4.3, 4.5, 4.0, 4.6, 4.2, 4.4]
email_scores = [3.8, 4.0, 4.1, 3.9, 4.2, 4.0]
phone_scores = [4.1, 4.3, 4.4, 4.2, 4.5, 4.3]

# Create your chart below



plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.lines) > 0, 'We could not find a boxplot. Did you use plt.boxplot()?'
labels = [tick.get_text() for tick in ax.get_xticklabels()[:3]]
assert labels == ['Chat', 'Email', 'Phone'], 'Set the x-axis tick labels to Chat, Email, and Phone.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Customer Satisfaction by Channel', 'Set the title to exactly "Customer Satisfaction by Channel".'
assert ax.get_ylabel() == 'Satisfaction Score', 'Set the y-axis label to exactly "Satisfaction Score".'
hints: A boxplot summarizes a distribution using quartiles and spread, which fits this comparison well.
Use `plt.boxplot()` on a list of score lists, then set the tick labels with `plt.xticks()`.

Try `plt.boxplot([chat_scores, email_scores, phone_scores])`, then `plt.xticks([1, 2, 3], ['Chat', 'Email', 'Phone'])`, `plt.title('Customer Satisfaction by Channel')`, and `plt.ylabel('Satisfaction Score')`.
solution_code:
plt.boxplot([chat_scores, email_scores, phone_scores])
plt.xticks([1, 2, 3], ['Chat', 'Email', 'Phone'])
plt.title('Customer Satisfaction by Channel')
plt.ylabel('Satisfaction Score')

title: Website Visits and Signups
markdown:
### The Scenario
A growth team wants a two-panel figure comparing daily website visits and daily signups over the same week.

### The Task
- Create a `1x2` subplot layout.
- In the first subplot, plot `days` vs `visits` and set the title to `Website Visits`.
- In the second subplot, plot `days` vs `signups` and set the title to `Daily Signups`.
- Set the first subplot y-axis label to `Visits`.
- Set the second subplot y-axis label to `Signups`.
- Display the figure.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

days = ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri']
visits = [120, 145, 138, 160, 172]
signups = [12, 15, 14, 18, 21]

# Create your figure below



plt.show()
validation_code:
fig = plt.gcf()
assert len(fig.axes) == 2, 'Create exactly two subplots.'
left_ax, right_ax = fig.axes
assert len(left_ax.lines) == 1, 'The first subplot should contain one line chart.'
assert len(right_ax.lines) == 1, 'The second subplot should contain one line chart.'
assert left_ax.get_title() == 'Website Visits', 'Set the first subplot title to exactly "Website Visits".'
assert right_ax.get_title() == 'Daily Signups', 'Set the second subplot title to exactly "Daily Signups".'
assert left_ax.get_ylabel() == 'Visits', 'Set the first subplot y-axis label to exactly "Visits".'
assert right_ax.get_ylabel() == 'Signups', 'Set the second subplot y-axis label to exactly "Signups".'
hints: This figure needs two side-by-side line charts, one for each metric.
Use a `1x2` subplot layout and place one `plt.plot()` call in each panel.

Try `plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)` with `plt.plot(days, visits)`, `plt.title('Website Visits')`, `plt.ylabel('Visits')`, then `plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)` with `plt.plot(days, signups)`, `plt.title('Daily Signups')`, and `plt.ylabel('Signups')`.
solution_code:
plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.plot(days, visits)
plt.title('Website Visits')
plt.ylabel('Visits')
plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
plt.plot(days, signups)
plt.title('Daily Signups')
plt.ylabel('Signups')
